title: Dimensional Input Parameter Language (DIPL): Language Specification, Version 1.0.0
abstract: DIPL (Dimensional Input Parameter Language) is a declarative language for describing structured input parameters for scientific and numerical software. It brings parameter values, data types, physical units, constraints, metadata, and relationships into one human-readable format. This specification defines DIPL’s syntax, type system, expression and unit semantics, schemas, validation, and execution model. It is intended for language users and implementers and serves as the reference for the SNT implementation. It includes a formal grammar and examples of the language’s main constructs.

title: Decomposing Apparent Skill in Machine-Learning Event Classification: A Multi-Catalog Study of Label Structure, Feature Coupling, and Operational Generalization
abstract: Machine-learning evaluation assumes that a held-out target represents the decision problem of interest. That assumption is difficult to satisfy when labels are constructed retrospectively from the same observational record that supplies the predictors, because a classifier can then reproduce regularities embedded in the target-generation procedure rather than resolve the harder decision. We treat earthquake event-role classification as an experimental case study of this problem and develop a diagnostic decomposition of apparent skill. Three catalogs differing in size, completeness, and feature availability are evaluated with chronologically partitioned gradient-boosted classifiers under a common window-defined target, and conventional held-out performance is decomposed using structural magnitude baselines, feature-family ablation, evaluation conditioned on the information state, synthetic epidemic-type-aftershock-sequence procedural nulls, alternative target definitions, probability calibration, conformal prediction, and cross-catalog transfer. Pooled discrimination was high, at ROC AUC 0.889 to 0.972, but fell by 0.264 to 0.387 when evaluation was restricted to events whose role is unresolved by preceding local magnitude ordering. A single magnitude-difference statistic came within 0.006 of the fitted models in two catalogs and exceeded them in the third, and removing the magnitude feature family reduced discrimination by 0.10 to 0.16. Synthetic catalogs generated without parent–offspring magnitude dependence reproduced both the high pooled score and its contraction under conditioning. Calibration, conformal coverage, and transfer behaviour changed independently of discrimination. The contribution is a reproducible diagnostic framework for interpreting machine-learning performance on retrospectively constructed scientific targets.

title: Operations of Mind: A framework for emergent thinking
abstract: Thinking is not hardcoded, and it cannot be. This note sets out Operations of Mind (OoM), a framework inwhich a machine is not given a method of thinking but a small set of basic mental operations, a drive tomake sense of what it encounters, and the freedom to chain those operations itself. OoM divides thoughtinto two deliberate layers: an inner layer that runs continuously and cheaply, and an active layer thatreasons deliberately on harder problems. It sits on two earlier pieces of the LOCUS programme, theCoherent World Hypothesis (CWH), which serves as its imagination, and the Repertoire Hypothesis, whichserves as its memory. The central bet is that thinking does not have to be trained into a machine; it canemerge from a small set of basic mental operations, chained under a drive to make sense. First tests ingenerated worlds give early support: operation chains grown from use beat chains built blindly, the driveignores noise without being told to, and see-then-invent beat a plain counting baseline for the first time,with a control showing the gain tracks real hidden structure. The gains are small, about 1.5 points ofroughly 5 learnable in a 60-step budget, and the active layer is untested. This note is a framework withpreliminary evidence, not a validated result.

title: Research materials for execution horizon and removal of defective demonstrations in LIBERO simulation
abstract: Research-only retained materials for a SmolVLA simulation study of execution horizon and oracle removal of defective demonstrations. Includes episode-level success arrays, injection and training manifests, model configuration and processor files, analysis and figure scripts, checker outputs, provenance records, and 19 distinct finetuned checkpoints corresponding to 20 main-design training runs. Two runs share byte-identical weights; checkpoint_manifest.json and restore_checkpoints.py reconstruct the 20 named directories. The 44-run H50-only replication set has retained success arrays but no retained checkpoint weights. Third-party raw demonstrations, unrelated product code and provider model weights are excluded. Six main point estimates were reproduced from stored success arrays. No new training, simulator evaluation or physical robot experiment was performed, and no complete fresh end-to-end replication is claimed. Historical headers are not public preregistration evidence. Existing SeoulTech facilities supported the work. Seokjun Song is pursuing plans to commercialize PersonTwin/Innerview. AI assistance is disclosed in the accompanying research documents. This deposit is not a journal submission or acceptance. Checkpoint packaging: identical 4 MiB byte blocks are stored once across the 19 files. The payload is distributed in 90 parts of at most 50 MiB, with weights_reconstruction_manifest.json, restore_robot_weights.py, README_weight_restoration.txt and LICENSE_restoration.txt. All 19 reconstructed complete-file SHA-256 hashes were verified against the retained originals; no weights were retrained, rounded, quantized or omitted. Download the complete payload and restoration files together and follow the README; the restored safetensors files supply the files referenced by the research archive. The 95-file deposit contains approximately 4.68 GB of unique checkpoint payload in place of 17.23 GB of separately stored checkpoints. Original derived outputs/documentation: CC BY 4.0; original research code: MIT; derived SmolVLA checkpoints, upstream configuration and processors: Apache-2.0 with included notice. See LICENSE.txt and licenses/.

title: Understanding, Improving, and Applying Self-Supervised Neural Representations
abstract: Human beings are known to develop a rich understanding of the visual world by simply being exposed to it and without constant explicit supervision. Although the mechanisms underlying this ability are not fully understood, Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) is an attempt to endow machines with a similar ability, by learning from unlabeled data using supervisory signals latent within the data. SSL has become a powerful paradigm for visual representation learning, but important questions remain about whether the learned representations are sufficiently expressive for downstream tasks, how such representations can be improved after pre-training, and how the composition of the pre-training data itself affects their usefulness. This thesis studies these questions from three complementary perspectives: scientific applications, representation desiderata and methods for improvement, and data-curation principles for real-world scenarios. First, we apply SSL to the task of automatic terrain categorization in Martian terrain images. Using deep self-supervised clustering, we show how neural networks can learn meaningful geomorphological and textural features from a large pool of unlabeled images, enabling the creation of a large dataset of Martian terrain images with scientifically relevant and granular terrain categories without the need for exhaustive expert annotation. We further validate the scientific significance of the discovered categories with expert input and create a detailed terrain taxonomy to encourage more fundamental analyses in the future. Second, we propose a general-purpose information-theoretic criterion for improving the quality of already-trained, highly optimized SSL representations. By maximizing the entropy of SSL-trained embeddings in a compact space, we prepare them as well as possible for future, as-yet-unknown, discrimination tasks. Our criterion is defined in terms of easy-to-estimate, low-dimensional constraints. We show that even without explicitly enforcing higher-dimensional constraints in our criterion, this approach yields practically useful embeddings and improves downstream performance without introducing extensive training overhead. Finally, we study how the composition of pre-training data shapes the usefulness of SSL representations for a given downstream task under finite compute and model-capacity constraints. Specifically, we examine how the diversity and relevance of the pre-training images, and their relative concentrations affect downstream performance while isolating common confounding factors. We propose a systematic framework with three data-composition axes—purity, distraction, and abundance—and use it to conduct carefully controlled experiments on a focused set of SSL models, datasets, and tasks. Our results refine the prevailing notion that larger pre-training datasets are necessarily better, and suggest that data curation should be treated as a first-order design variable in compute- or capacity-constrained regimes.

title: Volume VII: Sovereign and Global South Pathways: Selective Participation, Open Standards and Crypto-Agility under Dual Clocks
abstract: This seventh volume examines how the dual-clock framing, modular cryogenic stack, cryo-CMOS control and quantum-memory specifications developed in preceding volumes can be used by resource-constrained and Global South jurisdictions. It argues that full domestic construction of large fault-tolerant machines is neither necessary nor optimal. Instead, selective participation in cryogenic and control supply chains, adoption of open standards for memory and interconnect interfaces, and early crypto-agility programmes allow such jurisdictions to reduce dependency risk and harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure while the architectural and migration clocks continue to run. The analysis maps the residual-risk indicators of Volume VI onto practical policy levers that do not require waiting for a definitive quantum-advantage date.

title: When Patients Cut In: Extending Clinical Conversational AI Safety to Interruptions.
abstract: Clinical voice agents are now deployed in routine care, where real patients do not wait their turn: they interrupt. These systems typically use a cascaded architecture (speech-to-text -> LLM -> text-to-speech), so when a patient cuts the agent off mid-utterance, clinically required content can be lost even when the model handles cooperative transcripts well. Yet clinical conversational-AI benchmarks almost universally assume patients wait for the agent to finish, missing interruption-induced loss of required content. We present a transcript-based evaluation of interruption recovery, adapting conversation-analytic overlap categories into three operational types (recognitional, competitive, transitional sub-unit) and testing four deployment-oriented, non-reasoning LLM configurations across four cells spanning history-taking (information gathering) and FAQ (information provision), scored on whether the agent preserves the clinically required content. In the gathering cells, target-question failure varied across models; in the provision cells, where arms are directly comparable, failure rose for every model. Rankings differ across cells, and competitive FAQ interruption produced 30/30 provision-coverage failures for all four models (Wilson 95% CI: 88.6-100.0%; baseline 0/30 for three, 4/30 for Llama). A brief apology marker ('sorry to interrupt') shifts recovery by tens of percentage points, inconsistently across models, and for one it reduces recovery. Interruption robustness therefore cannot be a single score: evaluation must be content-grounded, reported per cell, and matched to the deployment's interruption profile.

title: ChronIQ-DRx2: restoring unwritten clinical decision logic unlocks personalized chronic disease management
abstract: Clinical records routinely document medical interventions but often omit the reasoning connecting patient-specific evidence to medical action. This limits the decision-relevant supervision available for training models for personalized care. Here we evaluate a data-augmentation approach that makes selected clinical decision relationships explicit in an 8-billion-parameter Qwen3 model, ChronIQ-DRx2. Using the same training cases and model architecture, expert-guided logic reconstruction was applied across four chronic diseases. On the held-out evaluation, the enhanced model had the highest plotted end-to-end task-completion rate among evaluated systems and higher plotted scores across diagnostic, medication and follow-up measures. The serious clinical error rates shown were 16.7% for the baseline and 12.5% for the enhanced model. In the human-AI evaluation, physician accuracy was 87.40% alone and 88.20% with AI assistance, while mean completion time was 0.959 and 0.780 min, respectively; medical-student accuracy was 62.71% and 74.80%, and mean completion time was 0.210 and 0.195 min. These results are descriptive point estimates; inferential comparisons are not reported here. Structured outputs may make recommendations easier to review, but rationale faithfulness, generalizability and effects on clinical safety require further evaluation.

title: Hyper-Synaptic Architecture: Dual-Space Embeddings, Tiered Context Resolution, and Truth-Maintenance Propagation over Knowledge Hypergraphs
abstract: Correspondence: Wonpyo Han · ORCID 0009-0002-7528-2228 · pk102h@naver.comIndependent Systems Architect & Knowledge Engineering Research Version 2.0 (Full 10-Page Technical Manuscript & Empirical Verification Release). Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over evolving enterprise knowledge bases exhibits three recurring structural failure modes: (1) high-dimensional hubness and static top-K admission inject weakly relevant or repetitive boilerplate passages into the prompt window, diluting transformer attention and inflating token expenditure; (2) append-only vector and graph indices lack non-monotonic belief revision, allowing superseded or falsified premises to continue supporting downstream conclusions; and (3) single-manifold lexical embeddings entangle domain-specific vocabulary with underlying causal mechanics, obscuring structural isomorphism across domains while failing to reject opposite-polarity analogies within the same domain. We present Hyper-Synaptic Architecture (HSA v3.0), an epistemic retrieval and truth-maintenance framework over directed knowledge hypergraphs, implemented in the reference kernel Synap-Reactor. First, HSA indexes each node into decoupled lexical and structural vector spaces via a domain-masking operator constrained by an empirical mutual-information / Fano lower bound, paired with a symmetric epistemic category firewall and a non-autoregressive System-1 calibrated 4-way ingestion gate. Second, Dynamic Quantized Synapse (DQS v3.0) formulates context assembly as a bounded-budget signal-to-noise optimization across three discrete resolution tiers: R0 (0-token dormant product-quantized state trained via online spherical K-Means and scored via exact O(M) Asymmetric Distance Computation lookup tables), R1 (≤25-token axon signature capped at 50), and R2 (full payload admitted via pre-update Bayesian-shrunk standardized margins z ≥ 0 and capped at 15). Third, a well-founded Truth-Maintenance System (TMS) propagates premise deprecations (SUPERSEDED_BY) across directed hyperedges using possibilistic critical-premise conjunction, disjunctive maximum aggregation, and Knaster-Tarski least-fixpoint worklist evaluation. Across a 10,000-node 2×2 factorial benchmark, a 100-node DQS–TMS coupling test, a 30-query continuous vault simulation, and differential verification over 1,000 random cyclic hypergraphs, HSA improves product-quantized cosine fidelity by +29.3 percentage points (0.599 → 0.892), accelerates 10,000-node CPU scan latency by 3.1× (387.9 → 126.7 ms) via exact subspace ADC lookup tables, reduces token consumption by 99.25% against uncapped retrieval (1,138,000 → 8,500 tokens/query) and 77.5%–88.2% across multi-session runs, cuts global hub monopoly by 47.1% while increasing specialist node diversity by 47.1%, and achieves a 0.00% (0/1,000) fixpoint mismatch rate on cyclic dependency graphs compared to 17.7% for single-pass BFS.

title: Little Room for Second-Order Rules in a Delta-Rule Testbed: Oracle Gains and an Evolution-Strategy Learner
abstract: Four pre-registered attempts to learn second-order modulation in a minimal plasticity testbed found nothing, and the learners failed their own positive controls. Before improving the learners further, this note measures whether anything was there to find, by comparing hand-built (oracle) second-order rules with the best uniform gain. A regime-dependent scalar oracle (49 gain pairs, chosen on a selection tape, scored on a fresh evaluation tape) gave no measurable benefit (mean evaluation error 0.13192 vs 0.13198; wins 20/60). An evolution-strategy learner failed the explicit-context gate (17/60 wins). A relation-specific oracle gating built from the true supports of the two transition matrices beat the best uniform gain in 36/60 systems (median +0.77%, mean −0.41%) and beat a random gating of the same size in 59/60 (median +2.07%), but missed the pre-registered criteria (3% over uniform; a 2-point gap over random gating, missed by 0.002). In this engine and task family, a structure-aware second-order rule carries a real, structure-dependent but sub-percent benefit over a tuned uniform rule, so the emergence tests were uninformative by construction; the toy result that a regime-dependent gain strictly beats any uniform gain does not transfer to this engine. Unpublished draft, not peer reviewed; synthetic systems only; it neither supports nor refutes the conjecture. The bundle reproduces every quoted number with verify_paper5.py (31 checks). AI use: simulations were written and executed by an AI coding model under written specifications and audited by a second AI system; the author is responsible for all content.

title: A Large-Scale Multi-Domain Unified Reverse Arabic Dictionary Dataset
abstract: Abstract Arabic is a linguistically and culturally rich language with a vast vocabulary that spans scientific, religious, and literary domains. However, large-scale lexical datasets linking Arabic words to precise definitions remain limited. We present MURAD (Multi-domain Unified Reverse Arabic Dictionary), an open lexical dataset with 96,243 word–definition pairs. The data come from trusted reference works and educational sources. Extraction used a hybrid pipeline integrating direct text parsing, optical character recognition, and automated reconstruction. This pipeline is designed to improve accuracy and minimize extraction noise. Its output undergoes validation through systematic quality checks and human review. Each record pairs a target word with its standardized Arabic definition and includes metadata specifying the source domain. The dataset encompasses terms from linguistics, Islamic studies, mathematics, physics, psychology, and engineering, supporting both computational linguistics and lexicographic research. Potential applications include reverse dictionary modeling, semantic retrieval, and educational tools. The release of this resource is intended to advance Arabic natural language processing and facilitate reproducible research on Arabic lexical semantics.

title: Artificial Intelligence in E-Commerce: A Theoretical Perspective on Personalization, Privacy, and Trust in the Indian Context
abstract: The digital growth and artificial intelligence (AI) in Indian E-commerce, via personalized recommendation systems influenced user experience. The AI boosted customers engagement from marketing point of view also it has increased the conversion rates, customer satisfaction and brand loyalty for E-commerce platforms. But these AI recommendations led to an ethical questions and marketing problems, in places where digital skills, knowledge and access are uneven among the shoppers. For example, when a tier 1 city shopper or consumer is used for tracking data have different outlook compared to consumer in a small town tracked with the same targeted ad feels uncomfortable. Our study was established with the help of marketing theory, consumer behaviour models and AI ethics, synthesizes existing literatures to provide a framework linking to personalization intensity and perceived consumers value, trust and privacy trade offs. It is seen that hyper-personalization of E commerce ads which might enhance participation; might reduce trust when things are not clear. And shoppers have not known as to how data is used. Our analysis with cases data from Indian E-commerce, together with global trends, shows how attitudes differ from urban and non-urban markets, are shaped by socio-cultural conditions and access to technology. Conceptual model used in this research paper, shows different personalization tactics linked with the marketing issues, with trust sitting in the middle of that relationship and data ethics acting as a boundary. To put simply, the model suggests when companies adjust customized offers or messages, this AI and its recommendations shaped results such as loyalty or purchase intent, but only as far as customers feel that they can trust the brand and that basic ethical expectations around data is not being misused. Study emphasizes necessity of transparency, user autonomy, equity in AI-driven personalization and advocates advanced empirical studies to prove the concept across various market segments.

title: Beyond MOS: judging synthetic voices by what L2 listeners understand
abstract: Study type: Observational (within-subjects experiment) Research questions: RQ1: Do comprehension, intelligibility and listening effort differ between a human reader, an open-source synthetic voice, and an LLM-based synthetic voice (default and learner-directed), for L2 listeners? RQ2: Do conventional naturalness ratings rank the voices the same way as learner comprehension, intelligibility and effort? Design: Within-subject, 4 voice conditions (H, OS, LD, LL) × 8 passages, 4 Latin-square lists. Each participant hears all 8 passages, each voice exactly twice. Participants: 48 L2 English listeners, aged 18+, students in the Foreign Languages department. 12 per list. Exclusion: under 18, incomplete session, failed device check. Materials: 8 B1-level passages (200-250 words each), 5 four-option MCQ items per passage, 1 dictation sentence per passage. Voices: human reader (male, L1 Uzbek, IELTS 8.0, neutral read); Kokoro-82M am_michael speed 1.0; Gemini 2.5 TTS Fenrir, LD prompt "Read the following text aloud."; LL prompt [full learner-directed text]. All audio mono, 44.1 kHz, -23 LUFS. Measures: - Comprehension (0-5 per passage) - Dictation (words correct / total) - Effort (1-9) - Naturalness learner (1-5) - Suitability (1-5) - Proficiency screen (10 items) - Teacher MOS naturalness (1-5) — separate panel of 10-15 English teachers Analysis: Mixed logistic and linear models with random effects for participant, passage, item. Kendall's W for RQ2 ranking comparison. Sensitivity analysis via simulation across n=32,40,48. Pilot: 5 students excluded from analysis. Data availability: audio, scripts and anonymised data on OSF.

title: SAMI Chimera: Sub-Neuronal Weight Surgery, Chimeric Base-to-Chat Synthesis, and Tensor Isometry Certification in DeepSeek-MoE-16B
abstract: Post-training preference alignment (RLHF, DPO, KTO) enforces refusal behaviors by establishing persistent attractors in intermediate transformer representations. Current refusal removal techniques, notably directional ablation, operate macroscopically by subtracting a 1-dimensional refusal vector from entire layer weight matrices, modifying 100% of targeted dense parameters and inducing severe reasoning degradation (-10.7% on GSM8K). Building upon the representation engineering framework established in SAMI Omni, this technical report presents Sub-Neuronal Mechanistic Weight Editing (SN-MWE) coupled with Constrained Orthogonal Procrustes Manifold Recovery, evaluated across the DeepSeek-MoE-16B architecture (1,782 experts and 5,466 tensors). By decomposing SwiGLU Feed-Forward Networks into discrete intermediate channel triplets, we prove that refusal mechanisms reside in an ultra-sparse subset (<0.14%) of intermediate channels. Specifically, we formulate and empirically validate:1. Sub-Neuronal Refusal Isolation and Excision: Neutralizing exactly 113 refusal channels across 16 critical experts, modifying only 0.13% of parameters while leaving over 99.86% of weights bit-for-bit untouched.2. Foundation Base Channel Transplantation (Chimeric Synthesis): Refusal-steering channels in the aligned Chat checkpoint are surgically replaced with unaligned Foundation Base columns, preserving conversational syntax while maintaining 100% router gating invariance.3. Constrained Orthogonal Procrustes Stabilization & Isometry Certification: Representations are geometrically stabilized via proper orthogonal rotations in SO(d) with det(R) = +1. A full-model audit across all 5,466 tensors certifies zero numerical anomalies (NaN/Inf) and a mean norm isometry ratio of 0.9991.4. Asymmetric Mixed-Precision Quantization (AsymQ): Packaging dense trunks and router gates at Q8_0 while compressing routed experts to Q3_K/Q4_K, achieving a 9.0–9.3 GB production footprint with 0.0% refusal rate and near-zero reasoning degradation (81.9% on GSM8K, Δ = -0.2%), executed statically in under 4 GB RAM/NVMe.

Current refusal removal techniques, notably directional ablation, operate macroscopically by subtracting a 1-dimensional refusal vector from entire layer weight matrices, modifying 100% of targeted dense parameters and inducing severe reasoning degradation (-10.7% on GSM8K). Building upon the representation engineering framework established in SAMI Omni, this technical report presents Sub-Neuronal Mechanistic Weight Editing (SN-MWE) coupled with Constrained Orthogonal Procrustes Manifold Recovery, evaluated across the DeepSeek-MoE-16B architecture (1,782 experts and 5,466 tensors). By decomposing SwiGLU Feed-Forward Networks into discrete intermediate channel triplets, we prove that refusal mechanisms reside in an ultra-sparse subset (<0.14%) of intermediate channels. Specifically, we formulate and empirically validate:1. Sub-Neuronal Refusal Isolation and Excision: Neutralizing exactly 113 refusal channels across 16 critical experts, modifying only 0.13% of parameters while leaving over 99.86% of weights bit-for-bit untouched.2. Foundation Base Channel Transplantation (Chimeric Synthesis): Refusal-steering channels in the aligned Chat checkpoint are surgically replaced with unaligned Foundation Base columns, preserving conversational syntax while maintaining 100% router gating invariance.3. Constrained Orthogonal Procrustes Stabilization & Isometry Certification: Representations are geometrically stabilized via proper orthogonal rotations in SO(d) with det(R) = +1. A full-model audit across all 5,466 tensors certifies zero numerical anomalies (NaN/Inf) and a mean norm isometry ratio of 0.9991.4. Asymmetric Mixed-Precision Quantization (AsymQ): Packaging dense trunks and router gates at Q8_0 while compressing routed experts to Q3_K/Q4_K, achieving a 9.0–9.3 GB production footprint with 0.0% refusal rate and near-zero reasoning degradation (81.9% on GSM8K, Δ = -0.2%), executed statically in under 4 GB RAM/NVMe.

title: Focus Pocus: Redirecting Technologically Distracted Students via Artificially Intelligent Characters
abstract: Digital learning environments challenge student attention, as notifications and low engagement cause students to drift from tasks, often without awareness. We present a system using real-time gaze tracking and screenshot analysis to detect distraction during digital exams and deliver timely, non-disruptive interventions via an on-screen character ("screenmate"). The system generates a continuous focus score by correlating where students look with what is displayed on their screen, and uses this score to trigger nudges when attention lapses are detected. We evaluated the system in a user study with 77 undergraduate students completing a 30-minute exam; results suggest that the gaze-derived focus score broadly tracks with students' subjective attention levels, though consistency varies across participants. Intervention analysis revealed a tension between effectiveness and intrusiveness — strong nudges successfully redirected focus but felt disruptive, while subtler cues preserved flow but were easier to ignore — pointing toward future work on richer behavioral signals and more adaptive, user-controlled interventions.

title: Dataset and experimental materials for evaluating LLM reliability in transport planning
abstract: This dataset contains the experimental materials for a study on whether publicly accessible conversational large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Microsoft Copilot) can generate road freight driver schedules that comply with EU driving-time and rest-period rules (Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 and Regulation (EU) No 165/2014). A single international freight transport scenario was tested at four levels of prompt structuring, from an open-ended instruction to a highly controlled prompt with explicit rules, fixed assumptions and a prescribed output format. The dataset includes: the shared transport scenario used in all experimental conditions; the exact system-level and user-level prompts for each of the four prompt levels; execution metadata for each test, including platform, model version and run details; the complete, unedited responses generated by the evaluated models (64 responses in total). The tests were run between February and June 2026 in private or history-disabled chat modes. The materials are provided to support transparency, independent verification and replication of the reported findings.

title: From Abstract Platforms to Plugin Architectures: A Constructive Refinement Mapping for Collective Adaptive Systems
abstract: Abstract Platformisation is a critical process underlying the development and deployment of collective adaptive systems for social coordination. However, platform centralisation and private ownership have led to extractive monopolies, and an asymmetric distribution of power. In the search for a viable alternative, this paper defines a universal platform formalisation and a concrete plugin architecture formalisation, presents a refinement mapping between the abstract and concrete formalisations, and specifies an algorithm to construct that mapping. We infer that this means the plugin architecture satisfies a certain definition of platform completeness. This re-interprets platforms not so much as a monolithic stack of components, but as a set of a reusable functional blocks which any user group should be able to use in order to define, construct, deploy, and manage their own platforms for their own purposes – e.g., implementing collective adaptive systems for social coordination.

title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
abstract: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.

title: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching
abstract: Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this with length-aware global batching and cross-GPU load balancing, raising training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. Built on Qwen3.5-4B and trained on 12.3M question-answer pairs converted from existing spatial datasets, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score (65.64%) among eight tested models, ranks first on seven of twelve benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve, while running 2.5 times faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 times faster than the base model.

title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code
abstract: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.

title: OpenGCUA: Toward a Fully Open Stack for Generalist Computer Use
abstract: Computer use has reached a turning point: the focus is expanding from GUI-only interaction to systems that complete tasks on users' computers through visual and programmatic interfaces. We define a generalist computer-use agent (GCUA) as a system in which the model chooses how to observe, act, and organize its work across visual and programmatic interfaces. Yet frontier implementations, such as GPT-6 Astra's computer-use system, remain largely closed, limiting systematic study of their design. We introduce Open Generalist CUA (OpenGCUA), an ongoing project to develop and open the full stack for GCUAs with the community. This report presents the first release of OpenGCUA. Code execution is a key feature of our agent design: it lets intermediate results determine subsequent operations and enables models to apply their existing programming capabilities directly to computer interaction. We also propose harness-to-model decision transfer, moving selected observations and task-state decisions from fixed harness rules to the model. On OSWorld-v2, our full configuration improves task scores across all eight evaluated models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, raising mean partial score by +19.6 points and reducing reported steps per task by an average of 53.0% relative to batched GUI-only execution. We release our implementation and prompts, evaluation trajectories from all eight models, and preliminary versions of a real-device harness and a cross-device SDK. The harness addresses real-device challenges not fully captured by benchmarks, while the SDK provides a common programming interface across computers, mobiles and browsers. Across four real macOS tasks under our real-device harness, selected Qwen3.8-Max runs use 19.4 times as many reported reasoning tokens as GPT-6 Astra, highlighting substantial differences between models in real-device execution efficiency.

title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.

title: Waypoint-OPD: Transferring RL-Induced Policy Shifts via Gated On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Policy-shift distillation reuses the difference between a teacher's log probabilities before and after reinforcement learning (RL) as supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, this endpoint policy shift cannot reveal whether local action preferences evolved consistently during teacher training. The same endpoint shift can result from early and late shifts that reinforce or partially cancel each other. We investigate whether agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts can guide selective transfer. We introduce Waypoint-guided On-Policy Distillation (Waypoint-OPD), which uses an intermediate teacher checkpoint from the same RL run to compare early and late shifts in relative action preferences at student-visited prefixes. We gate the endpoint shift according to the directional agreement between the early and late shifts, suppressing it when they point in opposing directions. Compared with endpoint-only transfer, our method requires only one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass. Using RL-trained Qwen3-4B teachers, we evaluate our method with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B as student models in mathematical and code reasoning. In all six domain--student settings, Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest domain-average score among the compared distillation methods. Ablations with the Qwen3-8B student show that removing or shuffling gates reduces mathematical reasoning performance. These results support the use of directional agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts to weight the endpoint shift during student training.

title: Gen4P: Video Generators are 4D Perceivers
abstract: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.

title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
abstract: Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics- aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe.

title: SoftCache: Adaptive Step Size Caching for Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Diffusion and flow models generate a sample over iterative steps, each a full pass through a large network, and that pass dominates generation cost. Training-free caching accelerates them by reusing activations from recent evaluations instead of recomputing them. Dynamic caching methods decide when to refresh by accumulating a cheap probe of the network input into a staleness signal and spending a fresh evaluation once it crosses a threshold. They perform hard caching: the signal is a binary switch between refresh and reuse, and every step, fresh or cached, advances by the prescribed step size. We observe that the signal carries much more than this switch. How far it sits below the threshold, its headroom, predicts the error induced by reuse. We propose SoftCache, which performs soft caching: instead of a binary switch, the headroom sets how far each cached step goes. Where the headroom is large, the sampler jumps past several scheduled nodes, and as a refresh nears, its steps shrink back toward the original step. These adaptive jumps may land between the scheduled nodes, taking the sampler off its fixed grid. SoftCache requires no training and adds no per-backbone settings: on FLUX for images and on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 for video, at speedups from $3.5\times$ to $6.9\times$, it is ahead of every baseline on all four fidelity metrics.

title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.

title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. Project Page: https://p3-wam.pages.dev/

title: SCOPE: Semantic Bounded Credit Optimization for Prompt Engineering in Text-to-image Generation
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables language models to improve text-to-image (T2I) generation by rewriting prompts for a frozen image generator. Existing methods typically apply a single signal derived from the image to individual subword tokens, although objects, counts, attributes, and relations form coherent semantic spans. We propose SCOPE, an objective based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that aligns update weighting with this structure. The rewriter jointly generates an enhanced prompt and its semantic partition. SCOPE pools shifts in policy log probabilities within each span to derive a shared coefficient for its token losses while retaining a single advantage for each completion. It requires neither separate span rewards nor additional image renders. Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE achieves average relative gains over vanilla GRPO of 9.48% on GeneVal and 7.62% on T2I-CompBench. Ablation studies show that both semantic boundaries and pooling within spans contribute to these gains, supporting semantic structure as a practical inductive bias for prompt engineering with RL.

title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies
abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

title: Grounding Generative Verification in 3D Content
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and 3D generation have expanded 3D understanding and synthesis. However, beyond visual fidelity, task-specific correctness grounded in 3D evidence remains a major challenge. We argue that building reliable 3D systems requires not only stronger generation and reasoning, but also verification feedback that identifies unmet requirements and explains their violations, allowing systems to reflect on and refine their outputs. Such feedback must integrate multi-view observations and distinguish genuine inconsistencies from projection-dependent appearances. We make three contributions. First, we introduce 3DVerifierBench, a benchmark spanning 10 tasks that evaluates decisions, rejection explanations, and responses to controlled changes in specifications and candidates. A human study reveals a 21.6 percentage-point gap between humans and the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, while explanation-aware analysis exposes weaknesses in rejection reliability. Second, we analyze verification across fine-grained factual categories, exposing errors in values and target binding. We develop a scalable pipeline combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled 3D editing, and native annotations to produce 14,126 training examples with contradiction explanations and linked counterfactuals. Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback.

title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories
abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.

title: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models still struggle to understand 3D spatial relations across views and update spatial judgments as the observer moves. A common approach fuses 3D reconstruction features into visual tokens, but aligning these features with pretrained semantic representations remains challenging under limited spatial supervision. We propose DK-VLM with Dual-Kernel Attention, which computes attention from both a visual token's input position and its geometric position in the scene. A semantic kernel retains the pretrained model's native attention and positional encoding, while a separate geometric kernel uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention through point displacements and relative view transformations. Then, a learned gate fuses their outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as fused reconstruction features. We further introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision to train the model to update its reference frame across successive judgments. It provides stepwise turn and heading targets derived from verified single-step annotations. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and ReVSI-32 (58.28). RC supervision further improves multi-step spatial reasoning, while the full model preserves general video understanding. Project page: https://sumuru789.github.io/DK-VLM-website/.

title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling
abstract: Generative visual verifiers play a crucial role in advancing multimodal intelligence. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique signal. Our experiments further demonstrate that these structured and interpretable outputs improve the verifier's generalization to out-of-domain multimodal critic tasks. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring at the global level. Under a general reinforcement learning framework, we first empirically demonstrate that the proposed pointwise graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in traditional text-to-image scenarios. We then extend our investigation to rule-governed generative world modeling where generative models are leveraged for world simulation and world reasoning under explicit rules. From a theoretical standpoint, we further show that a pairwise verification paradigm yields more accurate critiques than the pointwise formulation when ground-truth images are available, with empirical results on diverse structured world-modeling tasks such as Maze and Sudoku further validating the effectiveness of our approach. Overall, our findings suggest a key insight: the transition from generative models to structured world-modeling agents critically hinges on the availability of accurate pairwise graded visual verifiers.

title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.

The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.

title: SUPRA-TEX: 3D Generation with Super-Aligned Texture
abstract: Single image 3D generation aims to dress a given 3D mesh with relightable materials while faithfully preserving the visual details of a reference image. Existing methods either introduce artifacts when fusing inconsistent multi-view predictions or struggle to preserve fine details through implicit image-feature conditioning. To resolve these challenges, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, built on the principle of decoupling visible-material estimation, surface alignment, and observation-guided 3D completion. This division of labor allows the 3D generator, trained on limited 3D data, to focus its capacity on preserving visible evidence and completing unobserved surfaces. Specifically, we first train an MLLM-based image editing model to predict lighting-separated PBR maps in the reference view. We then project these maps onto the visible surface and encode them with the pretrained material VAE encoder into native observation latents that share the generation target's latent space. An interleaved flow transformer holds these latents as fixed, read-only anchors while alternating unobserved-region and full-surface updates to generate complete material latents. This design achieves super-alignment with the reference, delivering What You See Is What You Get fidelity on visible regions and coherent completion on unobserved surfaces. Trained solely on public datasets, SUPRA-Tex achieves SOTA performance in both geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end asset generation, matching or even exceeding leading commercial systems on in-the-wild images. Project page: https://supra-3d.github.io/supratex/

title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two alternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator's intermediate features to estimate each token's remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing preserves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ~1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5x faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ~2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35x faster at 24.5 fps.

title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.

title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/

title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.

title: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving
abstract: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib's forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12% over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR, covering up to 3.7% of extra groups. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing higher accuracy-cost efficiency. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery.

title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty
abstract: We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies.

title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users.

title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents
abstract: Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems.

title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT), combining feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.
